text: A structured piglet care program measurably increases piglet survival and the number weaned. Check breathing: clear mucus from the mouth and nostrils; weak piglets often recover some vigor after being dried and rubbed. Colostrum intake: colostrum (first milk, available only for a few hours) is rich in energy and antibodies — strong piglets nurse right away but weak ones may wander away from the sow, so it's crucial to make sure every piglet gets colostrum after birth. Nest preparation: piglets, especially at night, lose energy staying warm if cold, become too weak to reach the nipple, and a cold abdomen lets E. coli multiply and cause diarrhea — so a warm nest area matters a lot. Infection prevention: microbes (especially Streptococcus) can enter through the umbilical cord or wounds from teeth clipping/tail docking during the first day of life, potentially causing septicemia or arthritis. Anemia prevention: sow's milk doesn't supply enough iron, risking anemia, poor appetite, and slow growth — inject an iron supplement in the neck on day 2 of life, with a second shot 7–10 days later. Coccidiosis prevention: causes grey, hard-to-treat diarrhea around 7–15 days old (rarely fatal, but leaves piglets in poor condition at weaning); the only effective approach is preventive treatment with Toltrazuril 3 days after birth.
